original_question: Are cryptosystems built from infinite polycyclic groups resistant to quantum cryptanalysis? Equivalently, can one show that polycyclic group-based cryptosystems remain secure against quantum algorithms, especially given that no quantum algorithms are currently known for infinite groups?
target_in_paper: Section 5, open problem (10): "Are polycyclic group-based cryptosystems resistant to quantum algorithms?" The abstract states the same theme in a slightly narrower motivating form, emphasizing cryptosystems using infinite polycyclic groups and resistance to cryptanalysis on a quantum computer. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's post-quantum open problem, keeps the focus on polycyclic-group cryptosystems rather than a different group-theoretic complexity problem, and picks up the paper's motivating emphasis on infinite polycyclic groups together with the nearby observation that no quantum algorithms are known for infinite groups. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))
missing_details: The nearest official formulation is broader than your wording: the numbered open problem asks about polycyclic group-based cryptosystems in general, not only those built from infinite polycyclic groups. The latter appears in the abstract as the especially interesting motivating case. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))

The paper does not state any equivalence between "resistant to quantum algorithms" and "no quantum algorithms are currently known for infinite groups"; Section 2.6 gives the second statement only as surrounding motivation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))

The paper does not formalize "resistant" by a specific security definition, complexity class, adversarial model, or reduction; open problem (10) is posed informally as a yes/no research problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))

The scope is the class of polycyclic-group cryptosystems surveyed in Section 3, including key exchange, digital signature, authentication, and secret-sharing constructions, rather than one single named protocol. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))

No extra restrictions such as Hirsch length bounds, nilpotency assumptions, finite-vs-infinite platform distinctions inside the formal statement, or specified underlying search/decision problems are built into open problem (10); adding them would make the question narrower than the paper's official formulation. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))
refined_question: For the cryptosystems surveyed in the paper whose platform groups are polycyclic groups, determine whether they are resistant to quantum algorithms; in particular, decide whether cryptosystems using infinite polycyclic groups are resistant to cryptanalysis on a quantum computer. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))
justification: This is the closest paper-faithful refinement because the exact official statement is the numbered open problem in Section 5, while the abstract singles out the infinite-polycyclic case as the motivating special emphasis. Section 2.6 supplies the nearby context: the paper mentions quantum algorithms for several finite-group settings, then states that no quantum algorithms are known that apply to infinite groups. Since the paper does not supply a formal security model or prove any equivalence with a sharper reformulation, the draft should be tightened to the official yes/no question rather than broadened into a more general or claimed-equivalent statement. Also, this paper does not contain a relevant Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the operative target here is Section 5, problem (10). ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1607.05819))
